n: After chapter 7’s struggle comes this triumphant declaration: there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus and live by the Spirit rather than their fallen nature.

f.w: walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit

n: The principle of the life-giving Spirit in Christ has freed me from the grip of sin and death. One “law” overpowers the other.

f.w: the law of the Spirit of life
f.g: The governing power of the Holy Spirit that gives life.

n: The law couldn’t save us because our fallen nature made it weak. So God sent his own Son in a body like ours, as an offering for sin, and condemned sin in that very flesh.

f.w: in the likeness of sinful flesh

f.g: Passed sentence on sin itself, defeating it on its own ground.

n: He did this so the law’s righteous goal could be fulfilled in us as we live by the Spirit.

f.w: the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us

n: Those who live by their fallen nature fix their minds on its desires; those who live by the Spirit fix their minds on spiritual things. What we focus on shapes who we become.

f.g: Set their minds on, are preoccupied with.

n: A mind set on the flesh leads to death; a mind set on the Spirit brings life and peace. Book of Mormon prophets taught the same truth.

f.w: to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life

n: The fleshly mind is hostile to God; it doesn’t submit to his law and can’t on its own.

f.w: the carnal mind is enmity against God

n: Those controlled by their fallen nature can’t please God. The Joseph Smith Translation reads “after the flesh,” clarifying that Paul means living for the flesh, not simply having a body.

f.g: JST: “after the flesh” — living by fleshly desires.

n: But you are not ruled by the flesh but by the Spirit, if God’s Spirit truly lives in you. Anyone without the Spirit of Christ doesn’t belong to him.

f.w: the Spirit of God dwell in you

n: If Christ is in you, your body is still subject to death because of sin, but your spirit is alive because of righteousness.
And the same Spirit that raised Jesus will also give life to your mortal bodies — a promise of resurrection.

f.w: shall also quicken your mortal bodies

n: So, brothers and sisters, we owe nothing to our fallen nature — no obligation to live by it.
If you live by the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the misdeeds of the body, you will live.

f.w: mortify the deeds of the body

n: Everyone led by God’s Spirit is a child of God. Following the Spirit is the mark of God’s family.

f.w: led by the Spirit of God

n: You didn’t receive a spirit that makes you a fearful slave again, but the Spirit of adoption, by which we cry, “Abba, Father!” — the tender Aramaic word a child uses.

f.g: Aramaic for “Father” — the intimate word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36).

n: The Spirit itself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children. Latter-day Saints cherish this as a witness of our divine identity.

f.w: we are the children of God

n: If we’re children, we’re heirs — heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ — if we suffer with him so we may also be glorified with him. Latter-day Saint scripture promises the faithful “all that my Father hath.”

f.w: if so be that we suffer with him

n: Paul is convinced our present sufferings aren’t even worth comparing to the glory that will be revealed in us.
All creation is eagerly waiting, on tiptoe, for God’s children to be revealed in glory.

f.g: The creation — the whole created world.
Eager longing — literally watching with outstretched neck.

n: Creation was subjected to frustration and decay — not by its own choice, but by God, with hope in view.
Creation itself will be freed from its slavery to decay and share the glorious freedom of God’s children. Latter-day Saints teach the earth will be renewed and glorified.
We know the whole creation has been groaning together like a woman in labor until now. The pain is real, but it leads to new birth.
We who have the Spirit as a “firstfruits” — a first installment — also groan inwardly as we await our full adoption: the redemption of our bodies in the resurrection.

f.g: The first part of the harvest, a pledge that the rest is coming.

n: We were saved in hope. But hope that’s already seen isn’t hope — who hopes for what they already have?
If we hope for what we don’t yet see, we wait for it with patient endurance.

f.w: hope for that we see not

n: The Spirit helps us in our weakness. When we don’t know how to pray as we should, the Spirit pleads for us with groanings too deep for words.

f.w: we know not what we should pray for

n: God, who searches hearts, knows what the Spirit means, because the Spirit pleads for the saints in harmony with God’s will.
One of scripture’s most comforting promises: God works all things together for good for those who love him and are called according to his purpose.

f.w: all things work together for good to them that love God

n: Those God foreknew, he also marked out beforehand to become like his Son, so Christ would be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters. Latter-day Saints understand this as premortal foreordination, which still depends on our choices.

f.g: Mark out beforehand; Latter-day Saints speak of foreordination, not a fixed fate.

f.w: conformed to the image of his Son

n: Those he marked out, he called; those he called, he justified; those he justified, he glorified. Paul sketches God’s plan from premortal life to glory.
What then? If God is for us, who can stand against us? Paul moves into a hymn of confidence.

f.w: If God be for us, who can be against us?

n: God didn’t spare his own Son but gave him for us all. Won’t he also freely give us everything along with him? The greatest gift guarantees the rest.
Who can bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? It is God himself who declares them righteous.
Who can condemn? Christ died, rose, sits at God’s right hand, and pleads for us. Our Judge is also our Advocate.

f.w: at the right hand of God

n: Who can separate us from Christ’s love? Hardship, distress, persecution, hunger, poverty, danger, or violent death? Paul had faced nearly all of these.
Paul quotes a psalm: for God’s sake we face death all day long, treated like sheep for slaughter. Suffering for faith is nothing new.

f.w: we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter

n: No — in all these things we are more than conquerors through the One who loved us. We don’t merely survive trials; we triumph through Christ.
Paul is convinced that nothing — not death or life, angels or ruling powers, present or future —
— nothing high or deep, nothing in all creation, can separate us from God’s love in Christ Jesus our Lord. One of the most reassuring sentences in all scripture.

f.w: the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus
